Oreb
ō'reb
n. (one of the two princes of Midian slain by the men of Ephraim at Gideon's victory, and the rock named after him)
From Hebrew 'Oreb, a raven — the carrion bird, and a fitting name for a prince of the host that had eaten Israel bare for seven years. Not to be confounded with Horeb, the mount of God, which is a wholly different word.

Biblical Definition

Oreb is named with Zeeb in the rout that followed Gideon's three hundred, and the two are always spoken of together. The Ephraimites took the fords of Jordan ahead of the fleeing host and caught the princes: “And they took two princes of the Midianites, Oreb and Zeeb; and they slew Oreb upon the rock Oreb, and Zeeb they slew at the winepress of Zeeb, and pursued Midian, and brought the heads of Oreb and Zeeb to Gideon on the other side Jordan” (Jdg 7:25). The place kept the name of the man who died there, as places did — the rock Oreb stood as a marker in the land, and the memory outlasted the kingdom. Gideon used the victory to quiet Ephraim's jealous complaint with a soft answer: “God hath delivered into your hands the princes of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb: and what was I able to do in comparison of you?” (Jdg 8:3). Centuries later Asaph prays the same names over a new coalition: “Make their nobles like Oreb, and like Zeeb: yea, all their princes as Zebah, and as Zalmunna” (Psa 83:11), and Isaiah promises Assyria's overthrow “according to the slaughter of Midian at the rock of Oreb” (Isa 10:26). A dead Midianite chief became a permanent figure of speech for what God does to the enemies of His people.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no article for Oreb; in sacred history he is a prince of Midian slain by the Ephraimites, and the rock upon which he fell.

expand to see more

OREB, n. A raven; a prince of the Midianites in the days of Gideon.

He was taken at the passages of Jordan by the men of Ephraim and slain upon a rock.

The rock retained his name, and is called the rock Oreb.

His head and the head of Zeeb were brought to Gideon beyond Jordan.

The psalmist and the prophet Isaiah both allude to the slaughter at the rock of Oreb.

Key Scripture

Jdg 7:25 — "And they took two princes of the Midianites, Oreb and Zeeb; and they slew Oreb upon the rock Oreb, and Zeeb they slew at the winepress of Zeeb, and pursued Midian, and brought the heads of Oreb and Zeeb to Gideon on the other side Jordan."

Jdg 8:3 — "God hath delivered into your hands the princes of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb: and what was I able to do in comparison of you? Then their anger was abated toward him, when he had said that."

Psa 83:11 — "Make their nobles like Oreb, and like Zeeb: yea, all their princes as Zebah, and as Zalmunna:"

Isa 10:26 — "And the LORD of hosts shall stir up a scourge for him according to the slaughter of Midian at the rock of Oreb: and as his rod was upon the sea, so shall he lift it up after the manner of Egypt."

Modern Corruption

There is no significant modern redefinition of this name. The principle to recover is that Scripture keeps the memory of God's judgments as a ground of prayer, and that the church may plead old deliverances for present danger.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Oreb is a slain Midianite prince and nobody has contested him. What the rock Oreb sets against the modern habit of mind is the biblical use of memory. Asaph, facing a confederacy of ten nations, does not begin with strategy or with sentiment; he names a rock where God broke an army four hundred years earlier and asks Him to do it again. That is not nostalgia. It is the ordinary logic of covenant prayer: the God who acted is the God who is, and His past acts are the warrant for present petition.

The principle to recover is that the Christian remembers on purpose. Israel was commanded to set up stones and tell children what they meant; the Supper is kept “this do in remembrance of me” (1Co 11:24); the psalms rehearse the Red Sea in every generation. A church with no memory prays small prayers, because it has nothing to plead but the present. Oreb is a hard name and the deliverance was a bloody one, but Isaiah reaches for it when he wants to promise a frightened people that Assyria will fall too.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew 'Oreb (H6159), Oreb, a raven; 'oreb (H6158), raven, the bird; sar (H8269), prince, chief; tsur (H6697), rock; Midyan (H4080), Midian.

expand to see more

Hebrew 'Oreb (H6159) — Oreb; the prince and the rock alike.

Hebrew 'oreb (H6158) — raven; the carrion bird his name means.

Hebrew sar (H8269) — prince; the rank he held in Midian.

Hebrew tsur (H6697) — rock; the place of his death and his memorial.

Hebrew Midyan (H4080) — Midian; the oppressor broken by three hundred men.

Usage

"“They slew Oreb upon the rock Oreb” — the place named for the judgment done there."

"“Make their nobles like Oreb, and like Zeeb” — an old victory turned into a prayer."

"“At the rock of Oreb” — Isaiah's shorthand for the fall of an empire."
